power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Background: Dementia is frequently underdiagnosed in primary care, with fewer than half of cases identified and only 8-20% detected at early stages.

Our objective is to develop an Agentic AI-powered clinical decision support systems (CDSS) maintaining the patient's virtual cognitive status and provide physicians with ready-touse summaries and next step suggestions.
We developed MERIT (Multi-agent EHR-grounded Risk Identification and Tailored Care for Early Cognitive Decline in Primary Care) via participatory co-design with primary care provider.
It maintains a virtual cognitive status based on the patient's electronic health records (EHR) and conversation with the patient and provide clinical decision support based on it.
Retrieval augmented generation (RAG) was employed by the system to retrieve dementia-related risk factors from multimodal EHR.
Additionally, we used reflection Agentic AI design pattern to improve quality of AI Agent generated text.
We used one PCP's patient data to optimize the system, then used patients from another four PCPs for testing.
We mainly used expert manual evaluation based on 5-point Likert-Scales.
For readability of patient summary and personalized education material, besides manual evaluation, we also employed widely used Flesch Reading Ease and Flesch We-Kincaid Grade Level.
Results: MERIT has four modulars: 1) patient conversation agent; 2) patient virtual cognitive status maintainer; 3) personalized education provider; and 4) decision support provider.
Our evaluation focused on the providerfacing part, which relies on EHR without involving any patient conversation.
The evaluation on the testing data demonstrates good performance.

On a 5-point Likert scale, in the test set, patient virtual cognitive status summaries received average scores of 4.0 (SD 0.74) for correctness, 4.2 (SD 0.59) for completeness, 4.3 (SD 0.59) for readability, and 4.1 (SD 0.71) for clinical usefulness; clinical decision support received 3.9 (SD 0.87) for correctness, 4.3 (SD 0.66) for completeness, and 4.3 (SD 0.64) for adoptability; and the personalized education material received average ratings of 4.3 (SD 0.62) for completeness, 4.5 (SD 0.60) for readability, 4.3 (SD 0.78) for usefulness, and 4.4 (SD 0.49) for empathy.

Automated readability assessment showed that patient summaries had a mean Flesch Reading Ease score of 18.3 (SD 4.9) and a Flesch-Kincaid Grade Level of 13.7 (SD 0.7), consistent with college-level text, whereas personalized patient education had a Flesch Reading Ease score of 50.1 (SD 7.1) and a Flesch-Kincaid Grade Level of 11.7 (SD 1.5), which is high-school student understandable text.

Conclusion: Our developed system MERIT can maintain a virtual cognitive status based on the patient's multimodal EHR, provide the patient with clear and readable personalized education materials, and provide the PCP with ready-to-use cognitive summaries and decision support with high adoptability.
By integrating our CDSS into Epic in the near future, our developed system will largely benefit older adults with cognitive decline and slow down the progression.
Dementia affects more than 6 million Americans, and its prevalence is projected to increase substantially over the coming decades.

Early detection is critical for enabling timely interventions and potentially slowing disease progression; however, fewer than half of affected individuals are diagnosed at an early stage. [1] [2] [3] [4] This diagnostic gap is partly attributable to challenges in primary care, where the earliest symptoms of cognitive decline are often first recognized.
text.formatted: Early detection is critical for enabling timely interventions and potentially slowing disease progression; however, fewer than half of affected individuals are diagnosed at an early stage. <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">[1]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">[2]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">[3]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">[4]</ref> This diagnostic gap is partly attributable to challenges in primary care, where the earliest symptoms of cognitive decline are often first recognized.

text.text: Although primary care providers (PCPs) play a central role in the early identification of dementia, timely diagnosis remains difficult because of limited consultation time and the practical constraints of existing cognitive screening tools.

Widely used assessments, such as the Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE) and Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA), typically require 15-30 minutes to administer, making them difficult to incorporate into routine primary care visits.

These workflow constraints, combined with the complexity of dementia assessment and the expertise required for accurate evaluation, underscore the need for automated approaches that can support efficient, scalable, and timely dementia detection.
To help close this diagnostic gap, substantial research has focused on automating the detection of cognitive decline and dementia by mining data that clinicians already generate.

One line of work applies supervised machine learning directly to structured electronic health record (EHR) and administrative claims data: Nori et al. trained a gradient-boosted tree model (LightGBM) on claims and EHR features from more than five million individuals to predict incident mild cognitive impairment and dementia three to eight years before diagnosis, achieving over 80% area-under-the-curve (AUC). 5 A complementary and increasingly active line of work targets unstructured clinical notes using NLP.
text.formatted: One line of work applies supervised machine learning directly to structured electronic health record (EHR) and administrative claims data: Nori et al. trained a gradient-boosted tree model (LightGBM) on claims and EHR features from more than five million individuals to predict incident mild cognitive impairment and dementia three to eight years before diagnosis, achieving over 80% area-under-the-curve (AUC). <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">5</ref> A complementary and increasingly active line of work targets unstructured clinical notes using NLP.

text.text: Wang et al. developed a hierarchical attention-based deep learning architecture, combining a convolutional layer for local lexical patterns with a recurrent layer for sequential context, to detect evidence of cognitive decline in note sections preceding a formal MCI diagnosis at Mass General Brigham; the model achieved an AUROC of 0.971-0.997 across two independent test sets, outperforming keyword search and baseline classifiers (logistic regression, random forest, SVM, XGBoost). 6 Building on this deep-learning baseline, Du et al. subsequently benchmarked general-purpose LLMs against traditional machine learning and the deep-learning models, and found that LLMs, conventional ML, and deep learning exhibited distinct, largely non-overlapping error profiles on cognitive-decline classification, motivating ensemble strategies that combine their complementary strengths. 7 Other NLP-based approaches have extended detection to spontaneous speech, using linguistic and acoustic feature embeddings from connected-speech tasks to distinguish early, biomarker-confirmed Alzheimer's disease from cognitively unimpaired individuals. 8 Collectively, these approaches highlight the potential of using AI methods to detect cognitive decline automatically, providing supports for physicians and improving the efficiency.

text.text: Despite these detection-focused advances, few work has addressed how to deliver automated cognitive assessment within the practical constraints of primary care itself.
Efforts to close this gap have centered on brief, tablet-or app-based digital cognitive assessments (DCAs) designed to fit within routine visits.

In one large-scale implementation study, a DCA tool was integrated into workflows across seven primary care clinics using iterative, stakeholder-driven redesign together with a dedicated "brain health navigator" role to manage follow-up on positive screens, though overall screening completion remained modest (10.8% of eligible visits). 9 Other work has paired DCAs with machine-learning-based clinical decision support (CDS): a validation study of CDS recommendations generated by an ML-enabled DCA found that specialist reviewers rated most recommendations as clinically appropriate, and that primary care physicians using the tool reported minimal disruption to visit workflow. 10 Stakeholder-informed perspectives have further pointed to generative AI and LLM-based tools as a promising next step for extending these systems beyond one-time screening toward ongoing care-plan support, while cautioning that such tools remain exploratory and are not intended to replace clinician judgment. 11 Collectively, these efforts demonstrate that digital cognitive tools can be integrated into primary care with acceptable workflow burden, but current systems remain largely single-encounter screening instruments: they do not actively gather missing patient information over time, maintain a longitudinal memory of a patient's evolving risk profile, or simultaneously support both the patient and the provider throughout the diagnostic process.

text.text: Agentic AI, in which an LLM is orchestrated within an iterative reasoning-acting loop, such as the ReAct (Reasoning + Acting) framework, and given a tool-calling interface to invoke external functions, query databases, or trigger sub-agents, has recently emerged as a paradigm capable of addressing exactly these limitations. 12, 13 Unlike a single-shot LLM inference call, an agentic system maintains an explicit state (often represented as a graph, as in LangGraph-style orchestration) that persists across turns, decomposes a task into sub-goals, and routes each sub-goal to specialized agents or tools; safety mechanisms such as critic-in-the-loop self-verification and human-in-the-loop checkpoints are increasingly used to constrain agent outputs before they reach the patient or provider. 12, 13 Multi-agent architectures in particular have shown promise for improving reliability on clinical tasks through role-based specialization and cross-agent verification, and retrievalaugmented generation (RAG) over clinical guidelines and prior notes has been proposed as a grounding mechanism to reduce hallucination. 12, 13 However, recent systematic reviews and benchmarks emphasize that these architectures still require careful, task-specific evaluation rather than an assumption of automatic superiority over single-call LLM baselines, and that real-world clinical deployment and validation of agentic pipelines remains limited [14] [15] [16].

text.text: Agentic AI has begun to be explored in adjacent domains of longitudinal, relationship-based chronic care, such as psychiatric care, 17 but to our knowledge it has not yet been applied to longitudinal cognitive decline and dementia identification and management in primary care.
text.formatted: Agentic AI has begun to be explored in adjacent domains of longitudinal, relationship-based chronic care, such as psychiatric care, <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">17</ref> but to our knowledge it has not yet been applied to longitudinal cognitive decline and dementia identification and management in primary care.

text.text: To address this gap, we developed and evaluated an agentic AI-based CDSS, comprising a provider-facing agent, which are orchestrated around a shared, persistent virtual patient cognitive status as inter-agent memory.
Our developed system delivers actionable, longitudinally informed decision support to PCPs, significantly benefiting older adult patients.
>Methods
text.formatted: <head n="2." >Methods</head>

text.text: We developed an agentic AI powered provider-facing CDSS for early detection and monitoring of cognitive decline in primary care.
Python LangGraph was used for system development.
We co-designed it with a PCP (BL).

The system is implemented as a single FastAPI process serving a Vue 3 single-page application, with all components, including frontend, REST API, and inference server, co-located on one machine to support fully on-premises deployment in compliance with health-data privacy requirements.
Additionally, users can choose to use HIPAA-Compliant Azure OpenAI API or locally downloaded open-source LLM.
For our testing and evaluation, we mainly employed GPT-5.4 mini through MGB's HIPAA-Compliant Azure OpenAI service.
We also developed a graphical user interface (GUI) as a prototype.

LLM inference is served through a shared vLLM OpenAI-compatible endpoint, with differentiated agent behavior achieved through prompt engineering, tool bindings, and per-call temperature settings (0.7 for free-text patient dialogue; 0.1 or 0.3 for structured extraction, review, and report generation).
We used vLLM's Hermes parser for tool-calling, and used prefix caching to amortize the long, largely static system prompts emitted by each agent node.
Native tool-calling is enabled through vLLM's Hermes parser, and prefix caching is used to amortize the long, largely static system prompts emitted by each agent node.

Retrieval augmented generation (RAG) was employed by MERIT to retrieve relevant risk factors from longitudinal EHR as well as information from clinical guidelines in order to provide PCPs with accurate patient summary and decision support.

The study was conducted at Mass General Brigham (MGB), a large integrated healthcare system in Massachusetts, which has established secure, HIPAA-compliant environments for deploying and evaluating LLMs with real EHR data.
EHR Data were queried and pulled through Snowflake Enterprise Data Warehouse.
Patients were selected strategically by our PCPs.

Specifically, we only include patients with sufficient longitudinal histories (i.e., patients had more than 2 visits and one year history in the system) and excluded patients with limited relevant information, such as patients who were very healthy.
The study was approved by MGB IRB (2026P000189).

As illustrated in Table 1, we evaluated our system in terms of three aspects: 1) the performance of summarizing the patient's record for PCP to review before and during the visit; 2) the performance of generated patient education materials; and 3) the performance of decision support suggestions.
text.formatted: As illustrated in Table <ref type="table">1</ref>, we evaluated our system in terms of three aspects: 1) the performance of summarizing the patient's record for PCP to review before and during the visit; 2) the performance of generated patient education materials; and 3) the performance of decision support suggestions.

text.text: In terms of patient summary, we evaluated the correctness, completeness, readability, and usefulness using 5-point Likert-Scale.

We also applied Flesch Reading Ease (FRE) and Flesch-Kincaid Grade Level (FKGL) to evaluate readability as they are widely used automated evaluation methods for readability evaluation, and can provide an estimated education level for comprehend the text. 15 For decision support, we assessed correctness, completeness, and adoptability using 5point Likert-Scale.
text.formatted: We also applied Flesch Reading Ease (FRE) and Flesch-Kincaid Grade Level (FKGL) to evaluate readability as they are widely used automated evaluation methods for readability evaluation, and can provide an estimated education level for comprehend the text. <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">15</ref> For decision support, we assessed correctness, completeness, and adoptability using 5point Likert-Scale.

text.text: Finally, for patient education, we evaluated correctness, completeness, readability, usefulness, and empathy with 5-point Likert-Scale.
We also added FRE and FKGL for the readability evaluation.
We reported mean and standard deviation (SD) for evaluation scores.
The detailed evaluation rubric for the 5-point Likert-Scale is illustrated in the Supplementary Material Table S2.
text.formatted: The detailed evaluation rubric for the 5-point Likert-Scale is illustrated in the Supplementary Material Table <ref type="table">S2</ref>.

text.text: Our team has five physicians and each of them evaluated the agentic AI generated results for their own patients.
We firstly used one PCP's (BL) patients as the training set to optimize the system and the prompt iteratively, then used another four PCPs' patients as the external testing set.
Our optimized prompts are illustrated in the Supplementary Material.
Additionally, we conducted error analysis based on notes provided by PCPs during the evaluation process.
>Results
text.formatted: <head n="3." >Results</head>

text.text: As illustrated in Figure 1, MERIT mainly comprises four parts: 1) patient conversation Agentic AI system; 2) patient education Agentic AI system, which provides patients with personalized education materials based on their EHR; 3) provider Agentic AI system, which provides PCPs with patient summary and decision support; and 4) the patient's virtual cognitive status which is summarized from the patient's EHR.
text.formatted: As illustrated in Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>, MERIT mainly comprises four parts: 1) patient conversation Agentic AI system; 2) patient education Agentic AI system, which provides patients with personalized education materials based on their EHR; 3) provider Agentic AI system, which provides PCPs with patient summary and decision support; and 4) the patient's virtual cognitive status which is summarized from the patient's EHR.

text.text: The two tools were bounded to AI Agents: 1) RAG-powered EHR information retrieval and 2) RAG-powered clinical guideline search.

Notably, tools were bound with a ReAct (Reasoning and Acting) design pattern to improve performance. 19, 20 Detailed Direct Acyclic Graph (DAG) of the Agentic AI workflows are included in the Supplementary Materials.
text.formatted: Notably, tools were bound with a ReAct (Reasoning and Acting) design pattern to improve performance. <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">19,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">20</ref> Detailed Direct Acyclic Graph (DAG) of the Agentic AI workflows are included in the Supplementary Materials.

text.text: Modulars in MERIT are illustrated in Figure 2.
text.formatted: Modulars in MERIT are illustrated in Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">2</ref>.

text.text: Like Epic, MERIT contains a patient (or caregiver) portal and a provider portal.
Patient portal contains a conversation page, while providers can receive messages about the patient's cognitive status summary and decision support.

When MERIT feels it is time to check-in with the patient, it will direct the patient to the conversation page where the patient conversation agent AI system will ask the patient questions proactively to acquire cognitive status related information missing from the patient's EHR.
Additionally, the patient can click "View Personalized Advice" to get personalized advice.
The patient can also click "Review Summary Sharing with Clinician" to review and edit the summary before sending it to their corresponding PCP, which will protect the patient's privacy.
On PCP side, they can obtain the ready-to-use patient summary, which may be copied and pasted to the clinical notes before a visit, as well as the clinical decision suggestions.

Our evaluation focuses on the provider-facing part, which provides patient education materials, patient summary, and clinical decision support purely based on the patient's EHR without involving any patient conversation.

As illustrated in Supplementary Table S1, during evaluation we included 86 patients in total with 30 of them belonging to one PCP (BL) as the training set, which was used for prompt tuning and LLM optimization, and 56 of them belonging to four PCPs (MAL, MJR, DMR, ZEL) as the test set.

text.text: The expert evaluation for patient summarization, patient education, and decision support is shown in Table 3.
text.formatted: The expert evaluation for patient summarization, patient education, and decision support is shown in Table <ref type="table">3</ref>.

text.text: MERIT output received high ratings in both the training and test sets, with slightly lower scores in the test set (Figure 3), which is expected because the system was optimized on the training set and may be mildly overfitted to it.
text.formatted: MERIT output received high ratings in both the training and test sets, with slightly lower scores in the test set (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">3</ref>), which is expected because the system was optimized on the training set and may be mildly overfitted to it.

text.text: For patient summaries, mean ratings in the training set were 4.63 (SD 0.49) for correctness, 4.50 (SD 0.57) for completeness, 4.93 (SD 0.25) for readability, and 4.93 (SD 0.25) for usefulness; corresponding test-set ratings were 4.02 (SD 0.74), 4.18 (SD 0.59), 4.33 (SD 0.59), and 4.14 (SD 0.71).
Decision support was rated 4.70 (SD 0.47) for correctness, completeness, and adoptability in the training set, and 3.93 (SD 0.87), 4.25 (SD 0.66), and 4.26 (SD 0.64), respectively, in the test set.

For personalized patient education, training-set ratings were 4.30 (SD 0.47) for completeness, 5.00 (SD 0.00) for readability, 4.77 (SD 0.43) for usefulness, and 4.77 (SD 0.43) for empathy, compared with 4.25 (SD 0.62), 4.52 (SD 0.60), 4.31 (SD 0.78), and 4.37 (SD 0.49) in the test set.

Ratings were numerically lower in the test set for most dimensions, with the largest decline for decision support correctness (4.70 to 3.93), whereas patient education completeness remained stable (4.30 vs 4.25).
Automated readability metrics were consistent across the two sets.
Patient summaries had an FRE of 18.31 (SD 4.46) in the training set and 18.26 (SD 4.88) in the test set, with FKGL of 13.82 (SD 0.61) and 13.71 (SD 0.66), corresponding to college-level text.

Patient education was easier to read, with a FRE of 50.80 (SD 6.44) and 50.13 (SD 7.06) and an FKGL of 11.57 (SD 1.28) and 11.74 (SD 1.48) in the training and test sets, respectively, corresponding to approximately an 11th-to 12th-grade level.
Summarized comments from PCPs during the evaluation are listed in Box 1, Box 2 and Box 3.

PCPs identified the patient-facing recommendations (i.e., patient personalized advice) as the main strength of MERIT, describing them as easy to understand, useful, empathetic, and clinically grounded, and noting that they were personalized to details patients had shared, such as activities, family members, and pets (Box 1).
Decision support was considered specific and actionable, although occasionally incomplete (Box 1).
The PCPs also identified several areas for improvement (Box 2).

First, the system sometimes misinterpreted acute or remote events as current problems, for example by listing old or short-term medications (such as perioperative sedatives or brief opioid courses) as risk factors, or by referring to resolved injuries, while failing to incorporate chronic progressive conditions.
Second, the summaries relied heavily on detailed templated notes (e.g., nursing, therapy, and social work notes from hospitalizations), which may not reflect a patient's baseline status.

Third, some studies (e.g., HbA1c, vitamin B12, TSH) were reported as "not available" even though they had been obtained, and some of the available results were not expected to need repeating in a stable patient.
Fourth, nontraditional terminology was sometimes missed, such as stroke risk documented under "septic emboli to brain."

Finally, PCPs noted that MoCA or Mini-Cog was recommended for nearly all patients, including those with no evidence of cognitive impairment or minimal risk factors, and observed that guideline recommendations on screening of asymptomatic older adults vary.

In their overall observations (Box 3), PCPs felt that MERIT was most useful for patients with obvious neurocognitive decline and well-documented charts, and that it appropriately highlighted low-risk status in patients at low risk of dementia.

They considered the greatest potential value to be for patients with subtle cognitive decline or modifiable risk factors, while noting that improving accuracy and the use of clinical context would increase its utility in practice.
In this study, we developed an Agentic AI-powered CDSS named MERIT for cognitive monitoring in primary care.
Our CDSS was co-designed with PCP.
MERIT contains three modulars: patient personalized education, patient virtual cognitive status, and next step suggestions (or decision support).

Four PCPs evaluated the system using their own patients, which demonstrated that the decision support provided by MERIT had a high adaptability, and the personalized advice turned out to be highly useful and readable for patients.
Notably, MERIT has the potential to replace current labor-intensive and time-consuming cognitive tests in primary care, and patients can get high-quality advice without visiting a PCP.

While existing works of applying LLMs and Agentic AI to cognitive decline focus on automated phenotyping from clinical notes, 6, 7, 21 MERIT is a ready-to-use system assisting both patients and providers, and it was codesigned with PCP.
text.formatted: While existing works of applying LLMs and Agentic AI to cognitive decline focus on automated phenotyping from clinical notes, <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">6,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">7,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">21</ref> MERIT is a ready-to-use system assisting both patients and providers, and it was codesigned with PCP.

text.text: It extracts phenotyping from multimodal EHR (i.e., both structured data and unstructured notes), summarizes the patient's cognitive status, provides personalized education based on clinical guidelines, and provides high-quality decision support.
Notably, to protect the patient's privacy, MERIT asks the patient or caregiver to review and edit the cognitive status summary before sending it to the PCP.
A key challenge in employing LLM-powered agents is the inherent risk of hallucination, where the agent generates plausible yet inaccurate information.

This is caused by the stochastic nature of LLMs and raises the debate on whether LLMs truly reason or just memorize, with evidence from both sides. 22, 23 MERIT leverages RAG to check clinical guidelines and employes a reflection design pattern to mitigate hallucinations.
text.formatted: This is caused by the stochastic nature of LLMs and raises the debate on whether LLMs truly reason or just memorize, with evidence from both sides. <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">22,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">23</ref> MERIT leverages RAG to check clinical guidelines and employes a reflection design pattern to mitigate hallucinations.

text.text: Additionally, prompts of every LLM agent in MERIT were optimized using training data and through discussions with PCP.
The modular design of MERIT facilitates its future integration into Epic system.
Its patient-facing agent, provider-facing agent, and virtual cognitive status maintainer are decoupled components, so each can be connected to the EHR separately without redesigning the whole system.

Notably, integration of LLM-based tools into Epic is also already feasible in practice: LLM-generated draft replies to patient portal messages have been deployed within the Epic inbox and were adopted by clinicians. 24 Our study has several strengths.
text.formatted: Notably, integration of LLM-based tools into Epic is also already feasible in practice: LLM-generated draft replies to patient portal messages have been deployed within the Epic inbox and were adopted by clinicians. <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">24</ref> Our study has several strengths.

text.text: First, MERIT was co-designed by biomedical informaticians and a PCP, making it fulfill the PCP's and the patient's need.
Secondly, Five PCPs were involved in the system optimization and evaluation, with one of them involved in optimization and the other four involved in external testing.
Third, MERIT maintains a virtual cognitive status which was based not only on the patient's EHR, but also on the conversation with the patient.
Notably, the questions in the conversation were designed by MERIT itself according to the missing information related to dementia risk factors in EHR.

Fourth, MERIT is very useful in terms of 1) getting patients with understandable, complete, and accurate personalized advice, 2) summarizing the patient's cognitive status that a PCP can directly use when taking visit notes, and 3) generating decision support with high adoptability.
Finally, MERIT can not only be accessed by patients, but also be accessed by caregivers, so that older adults who are not familiar with digital products can still benefit from it.
Our study also has some limitations.
First, only PCPs tried our system and provided feedback, we have not obtained feedback from real patients.
Second, MERIT still needs to be optimized and improved, as PCPs pointed out several errors that are frequently made by the system.
Third, our evaluation was only based on the EHR of the patient.

In the future, we will work on integrating the system to Epic and make it ready to be used by patients and providers, and will evaluate and improve the system based on feedback from real patients and more providers.
In this study, we developed an Agentic AI powered provider-facing system, MERIT, which was co-designed by biomedical informaticians and a PCP.
MERIT can access the patient's EHR to collect dementia-related risk factors and provide the patient with personalized advice without the need to visit their PCP.

MERIT can also summarize the patient's cognitive status, and provide decision support to PCPs, helping PCPs to monitor the patient's cognitive status dynamically and saves their time to make clinical decisions.
MERIT maintains the patient's virtual cognitive status, provides high quality and understandable personalized advice to patients, and accurate decision support with good adoptability to PCPs.

In the future, we will integrate MERIT into Epic system to improve its usability and accessibility, and enhance it based on feedback from more PCPs and realword patients. and uses an agentic AI system (B) to extract risk factors for cognitive decline across 14 domains.

When the EHR lacks information on specific risk factors, MERIT identifies the gaps and initiates a conversation with the patient (E) to collect the missing information, which is then used to update the extracted variables.
The complete set of variables is used to generate a virtual cognitive status, a longitudinal, patient-level representation that is stored for reuse.
Based on these status and clinical guidelines, MERIT provides primary care providers with a cognitive status summary and next-step suggestions for decision support (C).
MERIT also generates personalized educational materials for patients based on their virtual cognitive status (D).

PCP comments related to strengths.
• Patient recommendations are excellent!

o I am very impressed with the patient recommendations. o These are easy to understand, useful, empathetic, and clinically grounded. o They even refer to specific activities, family members, pets etc. mentioned by patients -this is great!
• Clinical recommendations are still good, even if incomplete.
o The next step recommendations are still specific and actionable, even if occasionally incomplete.
PCP comments related to areas need improvement.

• Acute vs. chronic data and interpolation of past or noncontiguous events into current assessments o The AI summary frequently misinterprets acute events / medical encounters in the context of broader chronic medical problems and does not always incorporate key chronic progressive problems into assessments. o Examples:
Many patients have old meds listed as risk factors, including intra-operative or perioperative sedation medications and short term pain medication regimens that are years-old.
Acute traumatic injury with short term disabling injuries, opioid medications, etc.
Chronic progressive diseases (e.g. cancer) with heavy impact on cognition and ability to incorporate patient recommendations.
Referring to (now-resolved) mobility impairment documented in physical therapy notes from years-old injuries.

• Over-reliance on detailed and templated assessments (e.g. heavy use of nursing, PT, OT, nutrition, SW notes from hospitalizations). o It appears that the AI generated summaries heavily reference notes in the EHR where cognitive function, supports, etc. are described in depth. o This is not bad in and of itself but similar to the note on acute vs. chronic above may be out of context from the PCP's assessment. o Many, many of these assessments pull from inpatient hospitalizations where patient's had mental or physical status very different from their baseline.
• Inaccurate / missing retrieved data o There are many instances where studies (e.g.

A1c, B12, TSH) are listed as "not available" but were drawn, sometimes even frequently and recently. o Other times studies were drawn a little over a year ago but are labs like B12, A1c that may not be expected to rapidly change in an otherwise stable patient (i.e. it is reasonable that these may not have been retested annually). o I'm not sure the mechanism for why these are being missed -maybe they're not discussed in "notes" documentation and are being missed by natural language review?
o Many short term medications are being pulled in as meds needed for review -in many if not most situations they are not actually long-term active medications for patients.

• Mis-categorization when alternate/non-traditional nomenclature is used o Example: not listing stroke as a risk factor for a patient with serious debility due to a problem charted as "septic emboli to brain."
• MOCA or Mini Cog seems to be recommended for essentially all patients.

o This recommendation occurs even in patients with no evidence of neurocognitive dysfunction, minimal risk factors. o While cognitive assessment is a required part of Medicare annual wellness visits, there is no clear USPSTF recommendation for annual screening in most patients. o That being said, other guidelines like the International Associated of Gerontology and Geriatrics recommend annual cognitive screening in all patients >= 70 and the ACC recommends screening in "older adults with CVD."
text.formatted: o This recommendation occurs even in patients with no evidence of neurocognitive dysfunction, minimal risk factors. o While cognitive assessment is a required part of Medicare annual wellness visits, there is no clear USPSTF recommendation for annual screening in most patients. o That being said, other guidelines like the International Associated of Gerontology and Geriatrics recommend annual cognitive screening in all patients >= 70 and the ACC recommends screening in "older adults with CVD."

text.text: Box 3.
Other observations from PCPs.
• Unsurprisingly the AI summaries are best for patients with significant neurocognitive decline that is obvious to providers and has been worked up with significant chart documentation.
• For patients with low risk for dementia the tool also does a good job of highlighting low risk status and that general screening + risk factor modification is indicated.

• The challenge is the patients in the middle -and I imagine the best use for a tool like this would be identifying patients with subtle neurocognitive decline or significant modifiable risk factors o Overall I do think that the summaries, next steps, and patient recommendations are good for these patients but accuracy and appreciation of clinical context need to be improved for greater utility to PCP.

Overview of MERIT.
MERIT ingests longitudinal structured and unstructured patient EHR data (A)and uses an agentic AI system (B) to extract risk factors for cognitive decline across 14 domains.

When the EHR lacks information on specific risk factors, MERIT identifies the gaps and initiates a conversation with the patient (E) to collect the missing information, which is then used to update the extracted variables.

Based on these status and clinical guidelines, MERIT provides primary care providers with a cognitive status summary and next-step suggestions for decision support (C).
MERIT also generates personalized educational materials for patients based on their virtual cognitive status (D).
Figure 2.
MERIT System Illustration.
The overall design makes it easy to be integrated into Epic system.
(A) MERIT can initiate a conversation with the patient based on the patient's EHR to obtain additional dementia risk factor related information.
(B) The patient can request a summary of their virtual cognitive status summary, review it, edit it to remove sensitive information, and send it to their primary care provider (PCP).
(C) The patient can request a personalized advise, which is based on the virtual cognitive status.
(D) The PCP can get the patient summary and decision support.

Evaluation results (mean and standard deviation of scores) for generated content.
X-axis represents evaluation metrics; y-axis stands for detailed scores.
For each score, the left bar represents the performance on the training data (BL's patients) while the right bar represents the performance on the test data (patients from MAL, MJR, DMR, ZEL).
